self-concealing from one’s partner (i.e., not disclosing personal information, thoughts, and feelings to one’s partner) is associated with lower well-being in romantic relationships.
self-concealing from one’s partner, as well as being concealed by one’s partner, is associated with lower well-being in romantic relationships.

the association between self-concealments from one’s partner and one’s own and partner’s relationship well-being.
the association between self-concealments from one’s partner and relationship well-being, and the mediating role of basic needs.
the association between self-concealments from one’s partner and relationship well-being, and the underlying processes of this relationship.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-concealing one’s thoughts, feelings, and behaviors from one’s partner, and being self-concealing in general, is associated with lower well-being in one’s relationship.
self-concealing one’s thoughts and feelings from one’s partner has a negative association with relationship well-being.
self-concealing from one’s partner has a detrimental effect on the well-being of both the self-concealing partner and the partner of that individual.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
self-concealing from one’s partner may have detrimental effects on one’s own and one’s partner’s relationship well-being, and that this is due to thwarted basic needs.

self-concealing from one’s partner may be a risk factor for lower relationship well-being and that the underlying mechanism for this association is that self-concealers’ autonomy and relatedness need are not met by their partner.

self-concealing from one’s partner can be detrimental for one’s relationship well-being.
